angle: If your AI metrics don’t map to business KPIs, you’re measuring theater, not value.
sourceTitle: How to measure returns on AI
linkedinPost:
If your AI ROI deck talks about token counts, you’re measuring the wrong thing.

The Economist just outlined better ways to assess AI returns—moving from technical vanity metrics to business impact. That’s the shift enterprises miss most.

On programs that paid off, we started with a baseline and a control. Then we tied AI to 3–5 hard KPIs the CFO already cares about: cost-to-serve, containment rate, average handle time, NPS/CSAT, revenue per visit, backlog burn, time-to-resolution by segment.

We also priced risk, not just speed: precision/recall mapped to refunds, compliance breaches, or churn, with dollar values in the denominator. If a model improves deflection by 8% but increases escalations by 2%, the math decides—not the demo.

Finally, we tracked full costs: model calls, grounding data pipelines, human review, retraining, incident response. Many “wins” vanish when you add the last mile.

My rule: if the metric can’t move a budget line, it doesn’t belong on the AI scorecard. Make value boring, measurable, and defensible.

What KPIs would make your AI program CFO-proof? #EnterpriseAI #AITransformation #AIStrategy #CustomerExperience
